distribution.title:
The purpose of the data collection and generation is to provide a comprehensive, evidence-based analysis of how innovation and creative districts contribute to urban economic growth and broader urban development processes. The data is collected to assess the economic, social, cultural, and spatial impacts of these districts, including job creation, investment attraction, business development, social cohesion, cultural vibrancy, and quality of life. By systematically gathering and analysing data, the project seeks to understand not only measurable economic outcomes but also the underlying mechanisms through which innovation and creative districts influence urban transformation.

The data collection is directly linked to the overall objectives of the project, which aim to advance scientific knowledge in urban economics, innovation studies, and urban planning, while also generating practical insights for policymakers and urban development stakeholders. The collected data enables the testing of the project’s core hypothesis that innovation and creative districts act as catalysts for sustainable and inclusive urban economic growth. Furthermore, the data supports the development of innovative methodological approaches and the formulation of evidence-based policy recommendations, ensuring that the project’s outcomes are both scientifically robust and socially relevant.

The data collection and generation activities are closely aligned with the project’s work packages (WPs) and tasks, ensuring a structured and coherent research workflow. In WP1 (Literature review and methodological framework), existing academic literature, reports, and secondary datasets are analysed to define key economic, social, and cultural indicators and to establish a rigorous methodological framework for subsequent research stages. This work package ensures that data collection is theoretically grounded and methodologically consistent.

WP2 (Data collection and initial analysis) represents the core phase of data generation. During this phase, quantitative data is collected on key economic indicators such as employment rates, income levels, business growth, investment inflows, and real estate dynamics within innovation and creative districts. In parallel, primary qualitative data is generated through semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and stakeholder consultations involving policymakers, entrepreneurs, researchers, community leaders, and residents. This dual approach ensures that both statistical trends and stakeholder perspectives are captured, enabling a multidimensional analysis of district impacts.

In WP3 (Case studies and comparative analysis), the collected data is used to conduct in-depth case studies of selected innovation and creative districts across different geographical and developmental contexts. This work package focuses on analysing district-specific development trajectories, governance models, economic performance, and social and cultural outcomes. Comparative analysis across cases allows the identification of common success factors, contextual differences, and transferable best practices, directly supporting the project’s analytical and comparative tasks.

WP4 (Synthesis and dissemination of findings) integrates the quantitative and qualitative datasets generated in previous work packages. The purpose of data use in this phase is to produce scientifically sound conclusions, develop academic publications, and prepare policy briefs and dissemination materials. The synthesis of data ensures that research findings are coherent, comprehensive, and accessible to both academic audiences and decision-makers.

In WP5 (Elaboration of Horizon Europe project), the collected and analysed data serves as an empirical foundation for the development of future research proposals, demonstrating the relevance, feasibility, and impact potential of the research topic. Finally, WP6 (Project management) ensures continuous monitoring, quality assurance, and ethical compliance throughout all data collection and generation activities.

Origin of the data:
The data originates from a combination of secondary and primary sources, ensuring both breadth and depth of analysis. Secondary data includes official statistics from government and municipal databases, economic and policy reports, industry publications, planning documents, and existing datasets related to innovation and creative districts. Primary data is generated through original research activities, including semi-structured interviews, focus groups, ethnographic observations, field visits, and case study research conducted within selected districts. This mixed-origin data approach supports all project tasks across work packages and ensures that the research objectives are addressed in a comprehensive, reliable, and context-sensitive manner
